scope: Claim-level diagnostic workflow, nutrient-pattern, water-balance, light, root-zone oxygen, salinity, pH/water-quality, wound, and sampling evidence for the remaining unmapped Part 14 lessons.
rules: Symptom position, color, curl, necrosis, and wilt are observations with overlapping causes; they are not single-cause diagnostic tests.
Direct cannabis nutrient, light, temperature, and salinity experiments remain bounded to tested genotypes, root systems, treatment ranges, developmental stages, and methods.
General plant/greenhouse guidance may support mechanisms and sampling workflows but does not establish cannabis-specific injury thresholds.
All mappings remain pending independent science review.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Plant diagnosis is strengthened by symptom progression, whole-plant/site pattern, cultural history, affected-versus-unaffected comparisons, and representative confirmation rather than matching one image or symptom to one product.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Penn State Diagnostic Problem 101 progression/pattern/history workflow; Cornell abiotic-versus-biotic hemp pattern guidance.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports pattern-before-product differential diagnosis and explicit uncertainty.
claimEvidence.limitations: Pattern narrows a differential but does not by itself prove causation; mixed disorders and exceptions occur.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis responses to nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium supply vary with nutrient, genotype, growth state, tissue, and experimental context, so symptom age/location can guide a differential but cannot serve as a universal nutrient-photo key.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Saloner & Bernstein 2020 N study; Shiponi & Bernstein 2021 P study; Saloner, Sacks & Bernstein 2019 K genotype study.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports tissue-age and position as diagnostic observations requiring root-zone and environmental context.
claimEvidence.limitations: Controlled nutrient-response studies do not validate one symptom pattern as uniquely diagnostic in mixed production disorders.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis nutrient supply can alter chlorophyll-related physiology, morphology, ionomics, and growth, while similar chlorosis can arise from multiple nutrient/root/environment mechanisms; visual chlorosis therefore requires supporting measurements.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Direct N/P/K cannabis experiments plus Wee et al. cannabis/hemp nutrition review.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports chlorosis classification as a hypothesis generator rather than a diagnosis.
claimEvidence.limitations: Real production symptoms can be multifactorial and treatment thresholds from controlled trials are not universal.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Necrosis, scorch, and margin injury are nonspecific endpoints whose diagnostic value depends on progression, spatial pattern, exposure history, roots, environment, and signs of biotic agents.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Penn State diagnostic progression/pattern guidance; Cornell hemp abiotic-versus-biotic field guidance.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports differential diagnosis for irreversible necrotic injury.
claimEvidence.limitations: External injury pattern cannot reliably identify one chemical, nutrient, pathogen, hydraulic, thermal, or mechanical cause without corroborating evidence.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Leaf curling, cupping, clawing, twisting, and distortion are low-specificity observations; cannabis nutrient experiments demonstrate morphology changes with supply, but plant diagnostic guidance requires pests, pathogens, environment, roots, and management history to remain in the differential.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Penn State diagnostic workflow plus direct cannabis N/P/K studies.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports precise morphology records without slang symptom-to-cause shortcuts.
claimEvidence.limitations: No cited study validates a single leaf-shape pattern as a universal cannabis nutrient diagnosis.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis gas exchange and water use respond to interacting light and temperature, while plant root hypoxia can constrain respiration and uptake; wilting must therefore be interpreted as a supply-demand symptom with both dry-root and wet/hypoxic-root possibilities.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Chandra et al. 2008 controlled cannabis PPFD/temperature/CO2 gas exchange; Loreti & Perata 2020 plant hypoxia review.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports paired substrate/root/atmospheric measurements for wet-versus-dry wilt.
claimEvidence.limitations: Neither source defines a universal cannabis moisture or oxygen threshold for wilt across root systems.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Greenhouse edema can arise when water uptake exceeds transpiration under conditions such as wet root zones, high humidity, low light, cool air, and poor ventilation, but similar blistering/corking symptoms require pest, pathogen, spray, and other differentials.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Penn State Edema of Geranium cause/symptom guidance plus general diagnostic workflow.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the water-imbalance mechanism while explicitly marking cross-species transfer to cannabis.
claimEvidence.limitations: Direct cannabis edema research is sparse, so this mechanism is not cannabis-specific proof from appearance alone.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis morphology and canopy position respond to light environment, so elongation and stretch should be interpreted using measured photon environment, architecture, genotype, density, temperature, and developmental stage rather than a universal internode cutoff.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Rodriguez-Morrison et al. 2021 controlled indoor light response; Shape Matters 2021 architecture/light-gradient context.
claimEvidence.limitations: These studies do not define one PPFD or internode length that universally constitutes etiolation injury.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Low root-zone oxygen constrains aerobic metabolism and can contribute to impaired root function, while excess moisture and root disease can overlap; cannabis root-zone hypoxia diagnosis therefore requires oxygen/saturation/root/pathogen context.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Loreti & Perata plant hypoxia mechanisms; NC State hemp Pythium/excess-moisture context.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports oxygen-supply and disease differentials in saturated root zones.
claimEvidence.limitations: A universal cannabis dissolved-oxygen injury threshold is not established across substrates, temperatures, root densities, and genotypes.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Drug-type cannabis growth, physiology, yield, and cannabinoid concentration respond to NaCl stress in a root-system-dependent manner, demonstrating salinity and ion-specific stress while also showing that treatment response depends on solution context.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Yep, Gale & Zheng 2020 controlled hydroponic/aquaponic NaCl experiment.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports salinity/osmotic-stress diagnosis with explicit salt, EC, root-system, duration, and genotype context.
claimEvidence.limitations: The tested NaCl levels in one chemovar/system are not universal irrigation or root-zone injury thresholds.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Root-zone pH interacts with nutrient supply and ion availability, while irrigation-water alkalinity affects media pH buffering; pH-driven nutrient unavailability therefore requires method, water alkalinity, nutrient composition, medium, roots, and tissue context.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Shiponi & Bernstein 2021 P/root-zone pH responses; Wee et al. nutrition review; Penn State water-quality pH/alkalinity guidance.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports pH as one causal variable in a nutrient-availability differential rather than a universal lockout chart.
claimEvidence.limitations: No cited source defines one universal cannabis pH injury threshold across soil, peat, coco, hydroponics, and recirculating systems.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Irrigation-water pH, alkalinity, hardness, and EC describe different chemical properties and should be measured separately; alkalinity controls acid-buffering behavior and salts can accumulate with repeated irrigation.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Penn State 2025 Water Quality Toolkit sections on pH, alkalinity, hardness, EC/TDS, calibration, and records.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports water-quality records and separation of pH from buffering/salinity interpretation.
claimEvidence.limitations: General greenhouse screening ranges are not universal cannabis sodium, chloride, hardness, alkalinity, or salinity limits.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis architecture manipulation can change plant form and production outcomes, while general plant wound biology shows that tissue injury requires repair and functional recovery; visible attachment or swelling does not prove intact vascular or mechanical function.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Omary et al. wound/regeneration review; Danziger & Bernstein 2021 architecture studies.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports separating deliberate training architecture from unintended mechanical damage and monitoring recovery.
claimEvidence.limitations: Cannabis wound-biomechanics thresholds and load-bearing recovery are not well standardized; severe cases may require structural inspection.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Diagnostic quality depends on representative living samples, multiple symptom stages, roots when relevant, photographs, and contextual history; corrective action should be followed by repeat observation rather than treated as proof because an intervention was attempted.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Texas A&M Plant Sampling guidance; Penn State diagnostic workflow and recommendation for clinic confirmation when needed.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports case IDs, representative affected/unaffected sampling, preserved history, and verification after a controlled corrective action.
claimEvidence.limitations: Laboratory tests answer specific questions and can be non-diagnostic or incidental when specimen choice, timing, target selection, or interpretation are poor.
